assignments.title: 19.1 Critical Questions: Hesiod, Works and Days
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read each excerpt below and answer the question that follows it. Write three to five sentences for each answer, in your own words. Use evidence from the excerpt and from your lessons. If you are unsure about part of your answer, say so and explain what you would need to know. That is good thinking, not a mistake.

Excerpt 1

So there was never just one kind of Strife. There are two on the earth. One a man would praise when he understood her, and the other he would blame, for they have quite different hearts. One makes ugly war and fighting grow. She is cruel, and no man loves her, but men honor this heavy Strife because the gods require it.

The other is the elder daughter of dark Night. She stirs even the helpless man to work. A man grows eager for work when he looks at his neighbor, a rich man who hurries to plant and sow and put his house in good order. Neighbor competes with neighbor as he hurries after wealth. This Strife is good for men.

Hesiod, Works and Days, lines 11 to 24 (adapted from a public-domain translation)

Question 1. Hesiod says there are two kinds of Strife, which is the Greek idea of contest. Using what you learned in the lesson “Mountains and Sea: Why Greece Became Many Cities”, explain how Hesiod's good Strife differs from the contest Homer's heroes pursued, and why a city might want one kind and fear the other.

Excerpt 2

But those who give straight judgments to strangers and to their own people, and never turn aside from what is just, their city blooms, and the people in it flourish. Famine never keeps company with men who judge straight.

But for those who practice violence and cruel deeds, Zeus, who sees from far away, appoints a punishment. Often even a whole city suffers because of one bad man.

Hesiod, Works and Days, lines 225 to 231 and 240 to 241 (adapted from a public-domain translation)

Question 2. Imagine that the judges of a Greek polis began taking gifts from rich men and ruling in their favor. Using Hesiod's words and what you know about his quarrel with his brother, explain what Hesiod would expect to happen to that city, and what an ordinary farmer might do. Use what you learned in the lesson “Mountains and Sea: Why Greece Became Many Cities” to support your answer.

Your verdict

Question 3. Hesiod believes a city lives or dies by whether its judges are fair. Do you agree? Take a side, and defend it using Hesiod and the lesson “Mountains and Sea: Why Greece Became Many Cities”. Say what the strongest argument against your view would be.

assignments.title: 19.2 Primary Source Exercise: Plutarch, Life of Lycurgus
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read the passage below and answer both questions. Write one solid paragraph for each answer. We care more about how you reason than about which conclusion you reach, so show your thinking and use evidence from the passage and from your lessons. If you are unsure of something, say so.

Passage

Lycurgus made a rule that only iron money should be used. He gave it a small value for its great weight, so that a sum of ten minas needed a large storeroom in the house and a yoke of oxen to carry it.

When this money became the custom, many kinds of wrongdoing left Sparta. For who would steal it, or take it as a bribe, or rob for it, when it could not be hidden, could not be enjoyed, and could not even be cut up to any profit?

Plutarch, Life of Lycurgus, chapter 9 (adapted from a public-domain translation). Plutarch wrote many hundreds of years after the time of Lycurgus.

Question 1. Plutarch says iron money reduced wrongdoing in Sparta. Explain the reasoning behind his claim. Then use the lesson “Sparta: A Polis Built for War” to describe one other effect that iron money may have had on Sparta, even though Plutarch does not mention it here.

Question 2. Plutarch admits that no one agrees when Lycurgus lived, and he wrote long after. Choose one thing in this passage that you think we can reasonably trust and one thing we should question. Explain your thinking for each, and say what else you would want to know. Use what you learned in the lesson “Sparta: A Polis Built for War” to support your answer.

assignments.title: 20.1 Critical Questions: Aristotle on Solon
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read each excerpt below and answer the question that follows it. Write three to five sentences for each answer, in your own words. Use evidence from the excerpt and from your lessons. If you are unsure about part of your answer, say so and explain what you would need to know. That is good thinking, not a mistake.

Excerpt 1

Three of Solon's measures seem the most democratic. First and most important, he banned loans that were secured on a man's own person. Second, he allowed anyone who wished to seek justice on behalf of people who were wronged. Third, he gave the right of appeal to the jury-courts. They say this is what chiefly gave strength to the people, for when the people are master of the vote, they are master of the state.

Aristotle, Constitution of the Athenians, chapter 9 (adapted from a public-domain translation)

Question 1. Aristotle says the right of appeal to the jury-courts gave the people their chief strength. Explain why that right could matter so much to the thetes, who could hold no office, and what Aristotle means when he says that whoever controls the vote controls the state. Use what you learned in the lesson “Solon Weakens the Athenian Aristocracy” to support your answer.

Excerpt 2

I gave the common people as much honor as is enough, taking nothing from their dignity and reaching for nothing more. As for those who had power and were admired for their wealth, I took care that they too should suffer no insult. I stood with a strong shield in front of both, and I let neither side win unjustly.

Solon, quoted in Aristotle, Constitution of the Athenians, chapter 12 (adapted from a public-domain translation)

Question 2. Imagine that Solon had given the poor what they asked for and divided the land of the rich. Using this poem and the lesson “Solon Weakens the Athenian Aristocracy”, explain what you think might have happened to Athens, and why.

Your verdict

Question 3. Was Solon more a friend of the poor, a friend of the rich, or neither? Take a position, and defend it using the passages and the lesson “Solon Weakens the Athenian Aristocracy”. Say what the strongest argument against your view would be.

assignments.title: 20.2 Primary Source Exercise: Herodotus on the Athenians Freed
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read the passage below and answer both questions. Write one solid paragraph for each answer. We care more about how you reason than about which conclusion you reach, so show your thinking and use evidence from the passage and from your lessons. If you are unsure of something, say so.

Passage

So the Athenians grew in power. And it is clear, not from one example but in every way, that equality of speech is a good thing. While the Athenians were ruled by tyrants they were no better in war than any of their neighbors, but once they were rid of the tyrants they became by far the first.

This shows that when they were held down they fought below their strength, as men working for a master. But when they were freed, each man was eager to work for himself.

Herodotus, Histories, book 5, chapter 78 (adapted from a public-domain translation)

Question 1. Herodotus gives one explanation for why Athens grew strong after the tyrants. State it in your own words. Then use the lesson “Cleisthenes Invents Democracy” to explain which changes made by Cleisthenes could have produced the eagerness Herodotus describes.

Question 2. Herodotus praises equality of speech, yet the lesson “Cleisthenes Invents Democracy” reminds us that women, slaves, and foreigners living in Athens had no voice in the Assembly. Explain how both things can be true. Does the second fact weaken what Herodotus claims? Give your reasons.

assignments.title: 21.1 Critical Questions: Herodotus on Sardis
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read each excerpt below and answer the question that follows it. Write three to five sentences for each answer, in your own words. Use evidence from the excerpt and from your lessons. If you are unsure about part of your answer, say so and explain what you would need to know. That is good thinking, not a mistake.

Excerpt 1

It seems that it is easier to deceive a crowd than one man. Aristagoras could not deceive Cleomenes of Sparta, who was alone, but he deceived thirty thousand Athenians. The Athenians voted to send twenty ships to help the Ionians. These ships were the beginning of evils for Greeks and for foreigners.

Herodotus, Histories, book 5, chapter 97 (adapted from a public-domain translation)

Question 1. Herodotus blames the Athenian vote on a crowd being deceived. What does this suggest about how he viewed a large assembly? What might a defender of the Athenian Assembly say in reply, using what you know from the lessons “Cleisthenes Invents Democracy” and “The Ionian Revolt Against Persia and Darius’s Revenge”?

Excerpt 2

When Darius heard of the burning of Sardis, he asked who the Athenians were. When he was told, he asked for his bow. He set an arrow on it and shot it up toward the sky, and as it flew he said, "Zeus, grant that I may punish the Athenians."

Then he ordered one of his servants to say to him three times whenever his dinner was served, "Master, remember the Athenians."

Herodotus, Histories, book 5, chapter 105 (adapted from a public-domain translation)

Question 2. Suppose Athens had never sent the twenty ships to Ionia. Using this passage and the lesson “The Ionian Revolt Against Persia and Darius’s Revenge”, explain whether you think a Persian army would still have landed at Marathon in 490 BC, and what makes you more or less sure.

Your verdict

Question 3. Was the Athenian decision to help the Ionians wise or reckless? Take a side, and defend it using Herodotus and the lessons “The Ionian Revolt Against Persia and Darius’s Revenge” and “Marathon: Ten Thousand Athenians Against an Empire”. Say what the strongest argument against your view would be.

assignments.title: 21.2 Primary Source Exercise: Herodotus on Marathon
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read the passage below and answer both questions. Write one solid paragraph for each answer. We care more about how you reason than about which conclusion you reach, so show your thinking and use evidence from the passage and from your lessons. If you are unsure of something, say so.

Passage

Miltiades spoke to Callimachus: "With you now, Callimachus, it rests either to enslave Athens or to make her free, and so to leave behind for all time a memorial such as not even Harmodius and Aristogeiton left. For now Athens is in the greatest danger she has ever known. If she bows to the Medes, her fate is settled, for she will be handed over to Hippias. But if our city wins, she may become the first city of Greece."

The Athenians charged the foreigners at a run. They were the first Greeks we know of to charge at a run, and the first to bear the sight of Median dress and of men wearing it. Until then the very name of the Medes was a terror to the Greeks.

Herodotus, Histories, book 6, chapters 109 and 112 (adapted from a public-domain translation)

Question 1. Herodotus could not have heard the speech of Miltiades. Explain what a historian should do with a speech like this. Then explain how it connects to the idea in the lesson “Marathon: Ten Thousand Athenians Against an Empire” that one vote may have decided the fate of Athens.

Question 2. Herodotus says the Athenians were the first to charge at a run and the first to endure the sight of Median dress. Explain what this suggests about the part played by fear and confidence in the battle, and whether you think this mattered more than the Greek armor and spears. Give your reasons. Use what you learned in the lesson “Marathon: Ten Thousand Athenians Against an Empire” to support your answer.

assignments.title: 22.1 Critical Questions: Herodotus on the Spartans
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read each excerpt below and answer the question that follows it. Write three to five sentences for each answer, in your own words. Use evidence from the excerpt and from your lessons. If you are unsure about part of your answer, say so and explain what you would need to know. That is good thinking, not a mistake.

Excerpt 1

Demaratus, an exiled Spartan king, tells Xerxes about the Spartans: "They are free, but not wholly free. Law is their master, and they fear it far more than your men fear you. They do whatever it commands, and its command is always the same: not to flee in battle from any number of men, but to stay in their ranks and win or die."

Herodotus, Histories, book 7, chapter 104 (adapted from a public-domain translation)

Question 1. Demaratus says the Spartans are free, yet law is their master. Explain how a person can be both. Use what you learned in the lessons “Mountains and Sea: Why Greece Became Many Cities” and “The 300 Spartans at Thermopylae” about the phalanx to say why this kind of obedience might make an army stronger.

Excerpt 2

Before the fighting, a man from Trachis told the Spartan Dienekes that the Persian arrows were so many that when they shot, they hid the sun. Dienekes was not afraid. He made light of the number of the Medes and said, "Our Trachinian guest brings us good news. If the Medes hide the sun, we shall have our fight in the shade."

Herodotus, Histories, book 7, chapter 226 (adapted from a public-domain translation)

Question 2. Herodotus was not at Thermopylae and wrote about forty years later. Explain what this story shows about how the Spartans were taught to meet fear, and what its being a story told afterward means for how far we should trust it. Use what you learned in the lesson “The 300 Spartans at Thermopylae” to support your answer.

Your verdict

Question 3. Is it a virtue to obey a law that is also your master, as the Spartans did? Take a side, and defend it using Demaratus and the lessons “Sparta: A Polis Built for War” and “The 300 Spartans at Thermopylae”. Say what the strongest argument against your view would be.

assignments.title: 22.2 Primary Source Exercise: Aeschylus, The Persians
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read the passage below and answer both questions. Write one solid paragraph for each answer. We care more about how you reason than about which conclusion you reach, so show your thinking and use evidence from the passage and from your lessons. If you are unsure of something, say so.

Passage

The Persian queen asks about the Athenians: "Who is the master set over their army?" The chorus answers: "They are called the slaves of no man, nor the subjects of any."

A messenger describes the Greek battle cry at Salamis: "Come, sons of the Greeks! Free your fatherland, free your children and your wives, the temples of your fathers' gods, and the tombs of your ancestors. Now the fight is for all."

Aeschylus, The Persians, lines 241 to 242 and 402 to 405 (adapted from a public-domain translation). The play was first performed in Athens in 472 BC, eight years after Salamis.

Question 1. The play was written for an Athenian audience, yet these lines are spoken by Persians and about Persians. Explain what this choice suggests about how Aeschylus and his audience pictured the war. Why might showing the war from the other side make the Greek victory seem more meaningful? Use what you learned in the lesson “Salamis and Plataea: The Greek Victory” to support your answer.

Question 2. The battle cry says "the fight is for all." The lesson “Salamis and Plataea: The Greek Victory” says Greek unity was the exception, not the rule. Explain what would have to be true for "all" to be an accurate word, and point to a place where it strains.

assignments.title: 23.1 Critical Questions: Thucydides, The Funeral Oration
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read each excerpt below and answer the question that follows it. Write three to five sentences for each answer, in your own words. Use evidence from the excerpt and from your lessons. If you are unsure about part of your answer, say so and explain what you would need to know. That is good thinking, not a mistake.

Excerpt 1

Our form of government does not copy the laws of our neighbors. We are an example to others more than imitators of them. It is called a democracy, because power is in the hands of the many and not of the few. The law gives equal justice to all in their private disputes, yet the claim of excellence is also honored. When a citizen is distinguished in any way, he is preferred for public service, not as a privilege, but as the reward of merit. Nor does poverty stand in the way.

Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War, book 2, chapter 37 (adapted from a public-domain translation)

Question 1. Pericles says Athens is ruled by the many yet rewards merit. Do these two claims fit together, or do they pull against each other? Use what you learned in the lesson “From Delian League to Athenian Empire” about the lot, the juries, and pay for service to support your answer.

Excerpt 2

We alone regard a man who takes no part in public affairs not as harmless, but as a useless character.

Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War, book 2, chapter 40 (adapted from a public-domain translation)

Question 2. Suppose Athens had stopped paying citizens for jury service. Using this sentence and the lesson “From Delian League to Athenian Empire”, explain who might have stopped taking part and how that could change what Pericles is boasting about.

Your verdict

Question 3. Does a city that rewards merit and lets the many rule deserve admiration, even though many people were left out? Take a side, and defend it using Pericles and the lesson “From Delian League to Athenian Empire”. Say what the strongest argument against your view would be.

assignments.title: 23.2 Primary Source Exercise: Sophocles, Antigone
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read the passage below and answer both questions. Write one solid paragraph for each answer. We care more about how you reason than about which conclusion you reach, so show your thinking and use evidence from the passage and from your lessons. If you are unsure of something, say so.

Passage

Creon, the king, declares: "Whoever thinks a friend more important than his own country, I count him as nothing."

Antigone answers him: "I did not think your decrees had such power that you, a mortal, could override the unwritten and unshakable laws of the gods. They are not of today or yesterday, but live always, and no one knows from where they came."

Sophocles, Antigone, lines 182 to 183 and 450 to 457 (adapted from a public-domain translation)

Question 1. State in your own words what Creon puts first and what Antigone puts first. Then explain which of their claims you find stronger in the situation of the play, and what each would say is the greatest danger to a city. Use what you learned in the lesson “The Parthenon and the Theater of Dionysus” to support your answer.

Question 2. Thousands of Athenian citizens watched this play, and many also served on juries and voted in the Assembly. Imagine you are one of them. Explain how having seen the play might change how you judge a person who broke a law for a reason of conscience. Give your reasoning, not just your conclusion. assignments.title: 24.1 Critical Questions: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read each excerpt below and answer the question that follows it. Write three to five sentences for each answer, in your own words. Use evidence from the excerpt and from your lessons. If you are unsure about part of your answer, say so and explain what you would need to know. That is good thinking, not a mistake.

Excerpt 1

As for the reasons each side gave for breaking the peace, I have written them down, so that no one need ask how so great a war came upon the Greeks. But the truest cause, though the one least spoken of, I believe to be this. The Athenians were growing great, and this frightened the Spartans and forced them into war.

Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War, book 1, chapter 23 (adapted from a public-domain translation)

Question 1. Suppose Corcyra, Potidaea, and Megara had never quarreled with anyone. Using this passage and the lesson “The Road to War”, explain whether Thucydides would expect the war to have been avoided. What does your answer show about the difference between the spark that starts a war and the cause beneath it?

Excerpt 2

No fear of the gods or law of men held anyone back. As to the gods, people judged it was the same whether they worshiped or not, since they saw everyone dying alike. As to the law, no one expected to live long enough to be brought to trial and pay for his crimes. Each thought that a far heavier sentence was already hanging over him, and that before it fell he might as well enjoy something of life.

Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War, book 2, chapter 53 (adapted from a public-domain translation)

Question 2. Thucydides says the plague harmed Athens in another way besides sickness. Explain what he says broke down in the city, and why a city might depend on that even more than on good doctors. Use what you learned in the lesson “The Road to War” to support your answer.

Your verdict

Question 3. Who was more responsible for the war, Sparta or Athens? Take a side, and defend it using Thucydides and the lesson “The Road to War”. Say what the strongest argument against your view would be.

assignments.title: 24.2 Primary Source Exercise: Thucydides, The Melian Dialogue
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read the passage below and answer both questions. Write one solid paragraph for each answer. We care more about how you reason than about which conclusion you reach, so show your thinking and use evidence from the passage and from your lessons. If you are unsure of something, say so.

Passage

The Athenians say: "You know as well as we do that, in the world as it is, right is only a question between equals in power. The strong do what they can, and the weak accept what they must."

The Melians answer: "We trust that the gods will give us as good fortune as you, because we stand for what is right against what is wrong. And what we lack, we trust that the Spartans will supply."

Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War, book 5, chapters 89 and 104 (adapted from a public-domain translation). Thucydides says he gives the speeches as he thought the speakers would have spoken.

Question 1. State the Athenian argument and the Melian answer in your own words. Then explain what each side expected would happen next, and use the lesson “How Athens Lost the War” to tell what actually happened. Which expectation turned out to be closer to the truth, and why?

Question 2. Thucydides tells us he wrote these speeches as he thought the speakers would have spoken. How does that affect how far we can trust this passage as a record of what was really said? What can it still tell us about Athens and about Thucydides himself? Use what you learned in the lesson “How Athens Lost the War” to support your answer.

assignments.title: 25.1 Critical Questions: Plato, Apology of Socrates
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read each excerpt below and answer the question that follows it. Write three to five sentences for each answer, in your own words. Use evidence from the excerpt and from your lessons. If you are unsure about part of your answer, say so and explain what you would need to know. That is good thinking, not a mistake.

Excerpt 1

I went to one of those who seemed wise. When I examined him, I found that he seemed wise to many people and above all to himself, but he was not. I tried to show him that he thought he was wise and was not, and so I became hated by him and by many who were there.

I thought to myself: I am wiser than this man. Neither of us knows anything fine and good, but he thinks he knows something when he does not, while I, since I do not know, do not think I know. In this small matter I seem to be wiser, that what I do not know I do not think I know.

Plato, Apology of Socrates, around sections 21 to 23 (adapted from a public-domain translation)

Question 1. Socrates says he is wiser only because he does not think he knows what he does not know. Using the lesson “Socrates on Trial”, explain why the men he questioned might have been angry with him instead of thankful, and what that anger might have meant for Socrates years later.

Excerpt 2

Men of Athens, I honor and love you, but I will obey the god rather than you. As long as I breathe and am able, I will not stop practicing philosophy, urging and showing anyone I meet that he should care for the best state of his soul more than for money or reputation.

Plato, Apology of Socrates, around sections 29 and 30 (adapted from a public-domain translation)

Question 2. Socrates tells the jury he will not stop asking questions even if they order him to. Using the lesson “Socrates on Trial”, explain how this promise might have affected the vote of the jury. Then name one other factor from the lesson, apart from anything he said, that might also have mattered.

Your verdict

assignments.title: 25.2 Primary Source Exercise: Xenophon, Hellenica
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read the passage below and answer both questions. Write one solid paragraph for each answer. We care more about how you reason than about which conclusion you reach, so show your thinking and use evidence from the passage and from your lessons. If you are unsure of something, say so.

Passage

Almost everyone had supposed that if so great a battle were fought, those who won would rule and those who lost would obey. But the god so ordered it that each side set up a trophy as though it had won, and neither tried to stop the other from doing so. Each gave back the dead under truce as if beaten, and each took up its own dead as if victorious. Each claimed the victory, yet neither was seen to be any better off in land, in city, or in power than before the battle. There was even more confusion and uncertainty in Greece after it than before.

Xenophon, Hellenica, book 7, near the end of chapter 5 (adapted from a public-domain translation)

Question 1. Xenophon says people expected the winners of the great battle to rule and the others to obey. Explain, using what the lesson “Sparta’s Empire and Thebes’s Moment” says about Thebes and the other cities, why that did not happen.

Question 2. Xenophon admired Sparta, had known Socrates, and wrote about events he lived through. Choose one claim in this passage that you think we can reasonably trust and one that we should handle with care. Explain your reasoning for each. Use what you learned in the lesson “Sparta’s Empire and Thebes’s Moment” to support your answer.

assignments.title: 26.1 Critical Questions: Demosthenes, First Philippic
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read each excerpt below and answer the question that follows it. Write three to five sentences for each answer, in your own words. Use evidence from the excerpt and from your lessons. If you are unsure about part of your answer, say so and explain what you would need to know. That is good thinking, not a mistake.

Excerpt 1

No one should suppose that Philip can be stopped by hired soldiers alone. Men who fight for pay will serve whoever pays them. Let part of our force be our own citizens, so that the army belongs to us and has something of its own to defend.

Demosthenes, First Philippic (adapted from a public-domain translation)

Question 1. Suppose the Athenians had taken this advice and every citizen had served in the army. Using the lesson “Philip II and the Macedonian Machine”, explain one way this might have changed Athens's answer to Philip, and one reason many Athenians might still have refused to do it.

Excerpt 2

You Athenians behave like a barbarian boxer. When he is struck in one place, his hands go there. If he is hit somewhere else, his hands go there. He neither knows how to guard against a blow nor tries to look ahead. In the same way, if you hear that Philip is in one place, you vote to send help there. If he turns up elsewhere, you hurry after him. You never plan ahead.

Demosthenes, First Philippic (adapted from a public-domain translation)

Question 2. Demosthenes compares the Athenians to a boxer who only guards where he was last hit. In your own words, explain what he thinks the Athenians are doing wrong, and use the lesson “Philip II and the Macedonian Machine” to describe a habit that would have been a better answer to Philip.

Your verdict

Question 3. Was Demosthenes right that Athens should have fought Philip, or would peace have been wiser? Take a side, and defend it using the excerpts and the lesson “Philip II and the Macedonian Machine”. Say what the strongest argument against your view would be.

assignments.title: 26.2 Primary Source Exercise: Arrian, Anabasis of Alexander
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read the passage below and answer both questions. Write one solid paragraph for each answer. We care more about how you reason than about which conclusion you reach, so show your thinking and use evidence from the passage and from your lessons. If you are unsure of something, say so.

Passage

Parmenion, the older general, advised Alexander to attack the Persians by night. Their numbers were so great, he said, that the darkness would hide how few the Macedonians were, and the sudden attack would throw them into confusion. Alexander is said to have answered that he would not steal a victory. He wanted Darius to have no excuse for being beaten, and no way to blame the darkness or a surprise for his defeat.

Arrian, Anabasis of Alexander, book 3, chapter 10 (adapted from a public-domain translation). Arrian wrote many hundreds of years after Alexander.

Question 1. Explain the reasoning of Parmenion and the answer Alexander is said to give. What does Alexander seem to value more than a safe win, and what might he have risked by choosing it? Use what you learned in the lesson “Alexander Invades Persia” to support your answer.

Question 2. Arrian wrote many hundreds of years after Alexander, and he says only that the king is said to have answered this way. Explain how far you would trust this exchange as a true record of what was said, and what the story could still tell us even if the words are not exact. Use what you learned in the lesson “Alexander Invades Persia” to support your answer.

assignments.title: 27.1 Critical Questions: Arrian, Anabasis of Alexander
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read each excerpt below and answer the question that follows it. Write three to five sentences for each answer, in your own words. Use evidence from the excerpt and from your lessons. If you are unsure about part of your answer, say so and explain what you would need to know. That is good thinking, not a mistake.

Excerpt 1

Coenus spoke for the soldiers. "Sire, a ruler must know when to stop. You see how few of the Macedonians and Greeks who set out with you are left. Some were sent home, some died, and some, worn out or wounded, were left behind in the cities. Those of us who remain have no strength for more. All of us long to see our parents, wives, and children again. Go home, sire, and then, if you wish, lead another army."

Arrian, Anabasis of Alexander, book 5, chapter 27 (adapted from a public-domain translation). Arrian wrote many hundreds of years after Alexander.

Question 1. Using the lesson “The Conqueror and His Limits”, explain why the request of the soldiers was so powerful, and what it shows about what even a great king depends on.

Excerpt 2

Callisthenes spoke against the bowing. "Alexander, I think you worthy of every honor that a man can have. But honors for men and honors for gods have always been kept apart. Among the Greeks, no one bows down to a man. You came to add Asia to Greece, and you rule Greeks, so remember Greece."

Arrian, Anabasis of Alexander, book 4, chapter 11 (adapted from a public-domain translation). Arrian wrote many hundreds of years after Alexander.

assignments.title: 27.2 Primary Source Exercise: Asoka, Thirteenth Rock Edict
assignments.html:
Read today's primary source, then read the passage below and answer both questions. Write one solid paragraph for each answer. We care more about how you reason than about which conclusion you reach, so show your thinking and use evidence from the passage and from your lessons. If you are unsure of something, say so.

Passage

When he had been king for eight years, the Beloved of the Gods conquered Kalinga. A hundred and fifty thousand people were carried away, a hundred thousand were killed, and many times that number died. After that, the Beloved of the Gods felt deep sorrow for having conquered Kalinga, for when a land is conquered, the killing and the carrying away of people weigh heavily on him. He now holds that the best conquest is the conquest by Dhamma, which means right living. This conquest has been won here, and also in the lands on the borders, even where the Greek king Antiochus rules.

Asoka, Thirteenth Rock Edict (adapted from a public-domain translation). The king speaks of himself as the Beloved of the Gods.

Question 1. Asoka says he felt deep sorrow after the conquest of Kalinga and now values conquest by Dhamma more than conquest by war. Explain his reasoning. quizzes.title: 19.1 Reading Quiz: Mountains and Sea

questions.text: In Egypt and Mesopotamia, strong rulers gathered many towns under one crown. Why was that much harder to do in Greece?

answers.text: Greek farmers did not want to pay taxes to any ruler.
Mountains and islands split the land into small, separate areas, and there were no wide plains for an army to cross.
Greece had too few people to fill an army.
The Greeks did not have a common language.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Egypt and Mesopotamia grew up on wide river plains where a ruler could march an army across flat ground. Greece was cut into valleys and islands, so each place went its own way. The Greeks did share a language, so the last choice fails.

questions.text: A Greek traveler would say, "I am a citizen of Corinth," not "I am a citizen of Greece." What does this best show?

answers.text: Greeks did not care about their gods or festivals.
Greeks were ashamed of being Greek.
Corinth was the largest city in Greece.
A person's loyalty belonged first to his own city-state, not to a larger country.

questions.feedback_general: The Greeks shared a language, gods, and festivals, but not one government. Each polis guarded its own freedom, so people named their city as their home and their loyalty.

questions.text: Hesiod quarreled with his brother over land and then wrote a poem praising justice. What can we infer about why he valued justice?

answers.text: He had seen how much a farmer needs fair judges and honest neighbors in order to prosper.
He wanted to become a famous warrior like Achilles.
He believed that only kings could be fair.
He thought justice mattered less than glory.

questions.feedback_general: Hesiod was a small farmer who felt cheated in a land dispute. He believed cities with fair judges would prosper and cities with crooked judges would suffer. Homer's heroes, not Hesiod, chased glory.

questions.text: Hoplites bought their own armor. Why might a farmer-soldier begin to ask for a voice in running his city?

answers.text: Armor made him too heavy to farm.
He was a noble who wanted to be a king.
He risked his life and paid his own costs to defend the city, so he felt he had earned a say.
The city law required every hoplite to join the government.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says men who fought for the city often began to ask for a voice in running it, though this was never guaranteed and did not happen the same way everywhere. Fighting at one's own expense gave a farmer a reason to expect a share.

questions.text: Settlers from a Greek city found a colony in Sicily. Which description best fits the new colony?

answers.text: A province governed directly by officials from the mother city.
A new polis with its own laws and citizens that often kept friendly ties with the mother city.
A temporary camp that was abandoned after a year.
A city ruled by the king of Persia.

questions.feedback_general: A colony was usually independent, with its own laws and citizens, though it often kept ties of friendship and religion with the mother city. This is how Greek ways of life spread around the Mediterranean.

quizzes.title: 19.2 Reading Quiz: Sparta, a Polis Built for War

questions.text: Sparta took both the land and the people of Messenia. What does this tell us about the Spartans' situation afterward?

answers.text: They became the richest traders in Greece.
They no longer needed an army.
They freed the Messenians within a few years.
They lived among a large population they ruled by force and had to watch for revolt.

questions.feedback_general: The helots far outnumbered their Spartan masters, so Sparta lived in constant fear of a rising. Many historians think that fear shaped nearly every Spartan rule.

questions.text: Sparta had two kings, a council of elders, five overseers, and an assembly. What was the likely purpose of dividing power so many ways?

answers.text: To make sure that no single person or group could grab all the power.
To give the helots a chance to vote.
To let every person in the Spartan lands take part equally.
To avoid ever having to fight a war.

questions.feedback_general: Each part could slow down the others. Kings led the army but the overseers watched them, and the elders shaped the laws but the assembly could say yes or no. The helots and perioikoi had no vote.

questions.text: Why would a city that feared revolt raise its boys in the harsh agoge?

answers.text: Spartans did not value family life.
It needed soldiers who would obey without question and hold their place in the line.
The boys needed to learn how to farm Messenia.
The city wanted to teach its boys to seek personal glory above all.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says a city that fears revolt needs soldiers who obey. Spartans believed hardship made strong men, and strong men made a safe city. A Spartan was taught to put the city first, unlike Homer's glory-seeking heroes.

questions.text: The Spartiates did not farm or trade. Which fact from the lesson best explains how they were free to train for war?

answers.text: Iron bars served as money.
Spartan women ran the city.
Helots farmed the land and perioikoi made goods and traded.
The kings paid each citizen a salary.

questions.feedback_general: Because the helots farmed and the perioikoi made things, the Spartiates were free to train. The iron money was a separate fact about how Sparta discouraged trade.

questions.text: The lesson compares Sparta to a club with a very small membership. Which sentence best explains the comparison?

answers.text: Most people in the Spartan lands lived inside the city's walls but had no vote or share in ruling.
Anyone could join Sparta by paying a fee.
Sparta welcomed strangers and gave them citizenship.
Sparta had a very large citizen body.

questions.feedback_general: Only full Spartiates took part in the assembly. The perioikoi and helots lived in the Spartan lands with no voice. Sparta had answered how to defend a polis, but not who should share in ruling it.

quizzes.title: 20.1 Reading Quiz: Solon Weakens the Athenian Aristocracy

questions.text: Why did the debt crisis push Athens close to civil war?

answers.text: Foreign armies were about to invade.
Citizens were being made slaves by their own neighbors, and the poor were angry while the rich were afraid.
The nobles wanted to give all land to the poor.
The Areopagus had been abolished.

questions.feedback_general: A farmer who could not repay a loan could be seized and sold as a slave. The lesson says a city cannot hold together when citizens become slaves of their neighbors.

questions.text: The poor asked Solon to divide the land of the rich equally. He refused. What does this suggest about Solon?

answers.text: He was secretly on the side of the nobles.
He wanted to give everything the poor asked for.
He tried to stay between the two sides, giving neither all it wanted.
He did not understand what the poor wanted.

questions.feedback_general: Solon said he stood between the two sides like a boundary stone. Both sides trusted him partly because he was fair to each and gave neither everything.

questions.text: Before Solon, birth decided who could rule. After Solon, wealth did. Why did this change matter?

answers.text: A rich man from a family that was not noble could now rise, so more people had something to defend.
It made the aristocracy stronger than before.
It gave the thetes the right to hold the highest offices.
It ended the Assembly.

questions.feedback_general: The old aristocracy was weakened but not abolished. A man who could rise by the work of his farm had more reason to care about the laws. The thetes could attend the Assembly and sit on a jury, but not hold office.

questions.text: Why did the thetes, who could hold no office, still gain something under Solon?

answers.text: They received free land.
They became hoplites.
They could choose the archons.
They could attend the Assembly and sit on a jury that heard appeals, a small voice in the city.

questions.feedback_general: Aristotle says the laborers could attend the Assembly and sit on a jury that heard appeals. This mattered because it gave the poorest citizens a small voice.

questions.text: Peisistratus kept Solon's laws, lent money to poor farmers, and built temples, yet he was still called a tyrant. What does this show about the Greek word?

answers.text: A tyrant was always a cruel man.
A tyrant was a man who took power by force, whether or not he ruled harshly.
A tyrant was chosen by the Assembly.
A tyrant was a member of the Areopagus.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the word did not always mean a cruel man. A tyrant took power by force, and even a mild one took away the people's freedom to decide.

quizzes.title: 20.2 Reading Quiz: Cleisthenes Invents Democracy

questions.text: Sparta helped to drive Hippias out of Athens. What does the lesson mean when it calls this ironic?

answers.text: Sparta wanted Hippias to stay in power.
Sparta helped free Athens, yet Athens would grow into Sparta's rival.
Sparta gained control of Athens.
Hippias was a Spartan king.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson notes that Sparta helped free Athens while helping to make a rival. It is an example of events having results no one planned.

questions.text: When Cleisthenes was losing his quarrel with Isagoras, he brought the common people into his party. Why was this bold?

answers.text: Nobles could not speak to common people.
The people were all supporters of Isagoras.
Nobles usually settled such fights among themselves, and once the people tasted power they were unlikely to give it back.
It was against the law of Sparta.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says nobles usually kept their quarrels among themselves. Once ordinary Athenians had helped decide a struggle, they would expect to keep a voice.

questions.text: Why did Cleisthenes make each tribe a mix of people from the city, the coast, and the inland country?

answers.text: So that tribes could be ruled by nobles from each region.
So that no noble family could control a whole region, and men would think of themselves as Athenians first.
So that each region would have its own army.
So that the poorest citizens would be left out.

questions.feedback_general: Before, a noble could count on men of his own region to follow him. Mixed tribes meant a man from the coast worked beside a man from the city and the hills, and a shared loyalty helped hold the city together.

questions.text: Council members were chosen by lot, which means by drawing names. What does this method suggest about who could serve?

answers.text: Only men from noble families could serve.
Only the wisest man in each tribe could serve.
Only men who had fought at Marathon could serve.
Any citizen in the tribe had a chance to serve, not only the powerful.

questions.feedback_general: Fifty men from each tribe were chosen by lot to prepare business for the Assembly. Service did not depend on birth or power.

questions.text: The lesson says a good student of history holds two thoughts about Athens at once. Which pair matches the lesson?

answers.text: Athens was perfect, and Athens was ruined.
Athens made ordinary citizens part of ruling, and it kept most people who lived there out of it.
Athens had no democracy, and Athens had many slaves.
Athens was weak, and Athens was loved by Sparta.

questions.feedback_general: Only free men born in Athens counted as citizens. Women, slaves, and foreigners living in the city were left out. Both the new achievement and the limits are true.

quizzes.title: 21.1 Reading Quiz: The Ionian Revolt and Darius's Revenge

questions.text: Herodotus says Aristagoras began the revolt after his attack on Naxos failed. What does this suggest about his reasons?

answers.text: He was mainly guided by a plan to bring democracy to Persia.
He acted from fear for his own safety and from ambition, not from a grand plan.
He was ordered to revolt by the Spartans.
He wanted to give Miletus to Athens.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the revolt began from fear and ambition. Historians study the choices of individuals because small decisions can start great chains of events.

questions.text: Sparta refused to help the Ionians and Athens agreed. What best explains the difference in the lesson?

answers.text: Athens had no army at all.
Sparta was a friend of Persia.
The Spartan king heard that Persia lay three months' march from the sea, while the Athenian Assembly, new to Cleisthenes' system, said yes.
Athens had been conquered by Persia.

questions.feedback_general: The Spartan king refused because of the distance. The Athenian Assembly had been working for only a few years under Cleisthenes and voted to send twenty ships.

questions.text: Athens withdrew after the burning of Sardis and took no further part in the revolt. Why did Darius still want revenge on Athens?

answers.text: He wanted to punish Athens for the destruction of Sardis and to prevent any Greek city from helping his subjects again.
Athens had taken the Persian throne.
Athens had refused to trade with Persia.
Athens had killed his father.

questions.feedback_general: To Darius, Athens had joined his enemies and burned a city of his empire. He also wanted to make sure no Greek city would help his subjects rebel again.

questions.text: The lesson says Darius could not see the future. How does that detail help explain his decision?

answers.text: He knew Marathon would be a defeat.
He had already lost a war with Athens.
He expected a quick victory over one small city after crushing an empire's rebels.
He was too old to lead an army.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson explains that Darius expected an easy win. Understanding what people expected, not what we know came next, helps us see why they chose as they did.

questions.text: The Ionians lived inside the Persian empire but shared a language and gods with the Greeks across the sea. How did this help bring the two worlds into war?

answers.text: The Ionians had no interest in Greek affairs.
Persia and Greece had never met before.
The Ionians were forbidden to trade.
Being between the two worlds put them in a hard spot, and their revolt drew Athens and Persia into conflict.

questions.feedback_general: The Ionians had the culture of free Greek cities and the duties of Persian subjects. Their revolt came out of that tension and linked the two worlds.

quizzes.title: 21.2 Reading Quiz: Marathon

questions.text: The vote of the ten Athenian generals was tied. What was the effect of the war leader's vote?

answers.text: It ended the Persian war.
It brought Sparta to Marathon.
It decided that Athens would march out and fight instead of waiting inside the walls.
It chose Hippias as king.

questions.feedback_general: Callimachus cast the deciding vote for battle. The lesson says a single vote may have decided the fate of Athens.

questions.text: Sparta arrived only after the battle because of a religious festival. Why does the lesson call this a place where history turns on a small thing?

answers.text: The Spartans did not want to help.
If the festival had fallen on another date, Sparta might have fought beside Athens.
The festival was held in Athens.
Athens was not allowed to ask for help.

questions.feedback_general: The Spartans agreed to help but would not march until the moon was full. Contingency means events can turn on small facts like a date.

questions.text: Why did the Greeks choose to camp at the foot of the hills at Marathon?

answers.text: They wanted to be near their ships.
Persian horsemen could not easily reach them there.
The hills were sacred ground.
They hoped to hide from the Persians.

questions.feedback_general: The Battle callout says the Greeks camped at the foot of the hills, where Persian horsemen could not easily reach them. The Persians kept their ships on the beach.

questions.text: Heavily armed Greeks beat lighter-armed Persians at close range. Which detail from the lesson best supports this?

answers.text: The Persians had no ships.
The Greeks had archers on the hills.
The Greeks had trained to fight shoulder to shoulder and wore heavy armor and carried long spears.
The Persians were not allowed to fight at Marathon.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson ties the victory to the phalanx. Hoplites wore heavy armor and long spears, and each man trusted the man beside him. The Persians wore lighter gear with shorter spears and bows.

questions.text: The lesson calls the story of the runner who died after announcing the victory a legend. What does that label tell you?

answers.text: The story was written by Herodotus.
The story is proven false by archaeology.
The story is about Pheidippides running to Athens.
The story is told in later centuries and is not found in our main source, so historians mark it as a legend.

questions.feedback_general: Herodotus never mentions the run to announce the victory. He tells instead of Pheidippides' run to Sparta. Careful historians tell the legend but mark it as one.

quizzes.title: 22.1 Reading Quiz: The 300 Spartans at Thermopylae

questions.text: Xerxes had a canal dug at Mount Athos and bridges built across the Hellespont. What do these preparations suggest?

answers.text: He expected an easy, quick march.
He wanted to attack Persia's own cities.
He was planning the invasion with great care and expected to win.
He did not intend to enter Greece.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says everything about the plan said Persia meant to win. The canal avoided rough water where an earlier fleet was wrecked, and the bridges let armies cross on foot.

questions.text: Sparta was given command of the Greek alliance even though Athens had the biggest fleet. What can we infer?

answers.text: Sparta had the best soldiers, and Athens had to set aside pride for unity.
Athens had no ships.
Sparta had joined the Persians.
Corinth had been given command.

questions.feedback_general: Choosing Sparta made sense because it had the best land soldiers. The lesson says this showed how much Athens had to give up for the sake of unity.

questions.text: Why was the pass at Thermopylae a good place for a small Greek force to stand?

answers.text: It was close to Athens.
It was where the Persian fleet was anchored.
The pass was full of Greek allies.
The road was only wide enough for a few men, so the Persian army could not use its numbers.

questions.feedback_general: In a narrow pass only a few men can fight at a time. The lesson says the place did as much work as the men.

questions.text: Leonidas sent most of the allies away when he learned the Persians were behind him. What does this choice show?

answers.text: He wanted to hold the pass as long as he could so that others could escape.
He was afraid to fight.
He wanted to surrender to Xerxes.
He did not understand the danger.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Leonidas could have run but chose to stay. Courage of this kind is a virtue the Greeks admired and history remembers.

questions.text: The Greeks lost the pass. Which statement best explains why the lesson still treats Thermopylae as important?

answers.text: Xerxes turned back after the battle.
The stand showed Greeks would die rather than submit, gave time to prepare, and became a story that inspired courage.
Leonidas escaped and won the war.
The fleet at Artemisium won a clear victory.

questions.feedback_general: Artemisium was not decided. The value of Thermopylae lay in the time gained for evacuating Athens and preparing the fleet, and in the story told afterward.

quizzes.title: 22.2 Reading Quiz: Salamis and Plataea

questions.text: Athens spent the silver from the Laurion mines on ships, not on dividing the money among citizens. What was one lasting result?

answers.text: The city no longer needed soldiers.
The poorest citizens, the thetes, rowed the fleet and gained a new role in defending the city.
The Acropolis was protected from fire.
Sparta joined Athens.

questions.feedback_general: A trireme needed about two hundred men to row it, and the rowers were the thetes. A role in defending the city helped give them a bigger voice in governing it.

questions.text: Why did Themistocles want to fight in the narrow strait at Salamis?

answers.text: The Persian fleet could not use its large numbers there.
The Greeks had no ships that could sail in open water.
Xerxes had ordered it.
Sparta demanded it.

questions.feedback_general: In a narrow space the huge Persian fleet jammed together, and Greek triremes rammed them one by one.

questions.text: Why did Themistocles' trick against Xerxes work?

answers.text: Xerxes could not read the message.
The Greeks outnumbered the Persians.
Xerxes wanted to believe the Greeks were afraid and that a quick victory was waiting.
Xerxes had no ships left.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the trick worked because Xerxes wanted to believe it. An enemy's hopes can be used against him.

questions.text: At Plataea, Spartans, Athenians, and soldiers of many other cities fought together. Why does the lesson say this deserves to be remembered?

answers.text: It was the first time Spartans fought.
It ended the Olympic Games.
Athens had no part in it.
Greek unity like this was rare.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson calls this unity rare in the story. Many Greek cities sided with Persia or stayed out, and quarrels never fully stopped.

questions.text: What does the lesson suggest about Greek unity after the Persian danger passed?

answers.text: The Greeks stayed united for centuries.
Old rivalries returned, and Athens, now the great sea power, was proud and Sparta suspicious.
Sparta became the ruler of all Greece.
The cities joined into one country.

questions.feedback_general: The closing says the Greeks did not stay united for long. The same forces that nearly lost the war would return.

quizzes.title: 23.1 Reading Quiz: From Delian League to Athenian Empire

questions.text: Most league members stopped sending ships and sent tribute instead. How did this help Athens become an empire?

answers.text: Athens used the money to build more ships of its own, while members had no navy to resist it.
Members grew stronger than Athens.
The league moved to Sparta.
Members began to elect Athenian leaders.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Athens used the tribute to build more ships. A member that tried to leave, like Naxos or Thasos, was forced to stay.

questions.text: The lesson says that to members, Athens stopped being a partner and became a master. Which detail best supports this?

answers.text: The league treasury was kept on Delos.
Athens led because it had the biggest fleet.
Members still paid but could not leave.
Athens fought Persia.

questions.feedback_general: At first the league was a bargain. Once the danger faded, members were still paying and could not leave. Moving the treasury to Athens around 454 BC underlines the change.

questions.text: When Ephialtes took powers from the old council, who gained them?

answers.text: The kings of Sparta.
Cimon and his friends.
The archons.
The Assembly and the people's jury courts.

questions.feedback_general: In 462 BC the powers went to the Assembly and the jury courts, so the people had the final word. The rowers who saved Athens at Salamis could argue they had earned a larger share.

questions.text: Why were many officials chosen by lot and paid for jury service under Pericles?

answers.text: To keep the poor out of government.
So that anyone had a chance to serve, and a poor man could afford to take part.
To make the courts shorter.
To pay for the navy.

questions.feedback_general: Lot meant no one could buy an office. Pay meant a poor man could afford to serve. Many citizens learned how government worked.

questions.text: Athens gave more of its citizens a real part in ruling than Sparta did. What does the lesson still say about both cities?

answers.text: Both ruled without any slaves.
Both kept most of the people in their lands out of power.
Both had kings.
Both let women vote.

questions.feedback_general: Athenian citizens were free men with Athenian parents. Women, slaves, and metics were left out. Sparta also kept most people out of power.

quizzes.title: 23.2 Reading Quiz: The Parthenon and the Theater of Dionysus

questions.text: Pericles' enemies said Athens decorated itself with other people's money. What was that quarrel about?

answers.text: Whether Phidias was a good sculptor.
How far a ruling city may use the wealth of those it rules.
Whether marble was too costly.
Whether plays should be allowed.

questions.feedback_general: Part of the money came from tribute paid by allies. Pericles answered that Athens had done the work of defending Greece.

questions.text: A choregos paid for a chorus as a duty to the city. How did this put the Greek love of honor to public use?

answers.text: A rich man won glory by serving the whole city, so private ambition fed the city's pride.
It kept rich men from taking part in festivals.
It let the poor avoid paying taxes.
It ended competition among playwrights.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson contrasts this with the Homeric hero, whose glory belonged to one man. Here the old love of contest served the community.

questions.text: Antigone buries her brother against the king's order. What question does the play force the audience to face?

answers.text: Whether Athens should build a navy.
Whether a duty to family can outweigh the law of the state.
Whether Persia should be invaded.
Whether tribute should be paid.

questions.feedback_general: The play offers no simple answer. The lesson says such plays gave the whole city a chance to think about justice and duty together.

questions.text: A free city let Aristophanes mock its leaders in front of nearly twenty thousand people. What does this suggest about Athens?

answers.text: Athens ruled by fear.
Athens had no theater.
Athens allowed open criticism of its own leaders and thinkers.
Athens hated comedy.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson uses this to show that a free city let a playwright make fun of its own leaders, including thinkers like Socrates.

questions.text: Herodotus told stories with wonder, and Thucydides was stern and looked for causes. What did they give us together?

answers.text: A habit of asking what happened and why, by checking sources and searching for causes.
A single story about gods.
A list of Athenian laws.
A map of Persia.

questions.feedback_general: Before them the past was mostly told as myth or praise. The lesson says that habit is still the heart of history.

quizzes.title: 24.1 Reading Quiz: The Road to War

questions.text: Thucydides called the growth of Athenian power, and the fear it caused in Sparta, the truest cause of the war. What does this suggest about why the war began?

answers.text: Athens had attacked Sparta without any warning.
Corcyra had asked Sparta for help against Athens.
Sparta felt threatened by Athens as it grew stronger, even though Athens had not attacked it.
The cities of the Peloponnesian League wanted to join Athens.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Sparta did not need to be attacked to feel afraid. It was enough that Athens kept growing stronger. The quarrels at Corcyra, Potidaea, and Megara were the sparks, not the deepest cause.

questions.text: Athens made a defensive alliance with Corcyra and sent a small fleet. What was Athens most likely trying to prevent?

answers.text: Corinth gaining the large Corcyraean fleet.
Corcyra paying tribute to Sparta.
Corinth asking Athens to protect it.
Its own people moving to the island.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Athens did not want Corinth to gain Corcyra's ships. Corinth was an ally of Sparta and was furious, which is how a quarrel between two colonies became part of a larger crisis.

questions.text: Pericles told the Athenians to give up their land, move behind the Long Walls, and trust the sea. What did this plan depend on most?

answers.text: Spartan soldiers running out of food before winter.
Athenian hoplites beating the Spartans in an open field.
Persian help against the Spartan army.
Athens keeping control of the sea so that grain ships could still reach Piraeus.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Athens could not be starved out while its fleet kept the grain ships coming. If Athens lost the sea, the plan would fail. Athens could not beat the Spartans in an open field, which is why Pericles avoided one.

questions.text: Pericles asked farmers to watch their fields burn and not fight back. Why was this plan so hard to follow?

answers.text: The Long Walls were too small to hold anyone.
It asked proud citizens to accept real losses without striking back, and many wanted to march out and fight.
The farmers did not know where Piraeus was.
Sparta never burned any fields, so the plan made no sense.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the plan was sound but asked a great deal. Farmers saw smoke from their own burning fields and were told to do nothing. Pericles held them back, though not everyone loved him for it.

questions.text: Beyond the deaths it caused, what does Thucydides say the plague did to Athens?

answers.text: It made the Athenians trust their leaders more.
It sent the Spartan army home for good.
It weakened people's respect for law and the gods, because many thought they might be dead tomorrow.
It showed the doctors how to cure the fever.

questions.feedback_general: Thucydides says people began to lose their fear of the laws and of the gods. A city is held together by habits of duty and self-control, and when those fail the damage lasts longer than the sickness.

quizzes.title: 24.2 Reading Quiz: How Athens Lost the War

questions.text: At Melos, the Athenians argued that right and wrong matter only between equals. What danger does Thucydides want his readers to notice in that argument?

answers.text: Melos would soon be stronger than Athens.
Sparta had no reason to care about small islands.
The Athenian speakers were poor at arguing.
If the strong may do whatever they can, then no city is safe when it is the weaker one, even Athens.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says that if the strong may do whatever they can, no city is safe, not even Athens. Thucydides lets the story speak for itself and says that the next year Athens would learn that the strong do not always stay strong.

questions.text: Nicias warned that Sicily was too far away and the cost too high. Why was the expedition such a risky gamble?

answers.text: Sicily had no harbors that Athens could use.
It was a very long sail from home, so supplies and help were hard to send, and Athens staked its whole fleet on it.
Syracuse was already an ally of Athens.
Athens had no money to pay for any ships.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson stresses that food and supplies had to cross a long stretch of sea, and that any mistake would be costly. An attack there was a gamble with the city's whole fleet.

questions.text: Alcibiades was called home for trial, ran away to Sparta, and advised the Spartans. What can we infer from this?

answers.text: Sparta had no interest in what Athens was doing.
Alcibiades had been loyal to Sparta since boyhood.
A city can be badly hurt when a gifted man it has turned against goes over to its enemy.
The Spartans did not take his advice.

questions.feedback_general: Alcibiades told Sparta to send a commander to Syracuse and to fortify a place inside Athenian land. Sparta did both. The lesson says this helped bring the expedition down and kept Athens under pressure all year long.

questions.text: Sparta had fought Persia at Thermopylae, yet later took Persian gold. What did the gold give Sparta?

answers.text: A fleet and crews, which Sparta had always lacked.
Better hoplites than Athens could train.
The Long Walls of Athens.
A peace that lasted fifty years.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Spartans had never before been a sea power. With Persian money they built a fleet, and Lysander got still more money from a Persian prince. In return, Persia wanted the Greek cities of Asia Minor.

questions.text: At Aegospotami, Lysander captured almost every Athenian ship. What mistake made this possible?

answers.text: The Athenian ships were too slow to leave the harbor.
Lysander had a much larger fleet than Athens.
Alcibiades sailed over to the Spartans.
The Athenian crews went ashore for food and were scattered, and they ignored a warning to move to a safer place.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Lysander sailed over while the crews were scattered on the shore. Alcibiades, who lived nearby, is said to have warned them, but they ignored him.

quizzes.title: 25.1 Reading Quiz: Socrates on Trial

questions.text: After the Thirty fell, Athenian citizens swore not to punish each other for what had been done during the war and the tyranny. What was the purpose of this amnesty?

answers.text: To heal the city and keep old quarrels from tearing it apart.
To bring the Thirty back into power.
To repay the debt that Athens owed Sparta.
To punish everyone who had fought for the Thirty.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the amnesty was meant to heal the city. It also had a side effect that matters later, because it may have shaped the charges brought against Socrates.

questions.text: The oracle at Delphi said that no one was wiser than Socrates, and he went looking for someone who was. What did he decide in the end?

answers.text: That he had read more books than anyone else.
That he had won more battles than anyone else.
That he was wiser only in one way: he knew that he did not know.
That the oracle had made a mistake and should be ignored.

questions.feedback_general: In Plato's account, Socrates questioned famous men and found that those who sounded certain could not explain their own words. He decided he was wiser only in this: he knew that he did not know.

questions.text: Anytus, one of the accusers, had fought against the Thirty. What does this suggest about the men who brought Socrates to court?

answers.text: They were secretly friends of Critias.
They may have honestly feared that his questions and his students had harmed the democracy.
They had been paid by Sparta to remove him.
They wanted Plato to rule Athens.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the accusers were not tyrants but democrats who loved their city. It was in some ways a trial of how far a democracy can allow questioning.

questions.text: Some historians think the charge about the gods was used to get around the amnesty. What is the reasoning?

answers.text: The jury cared only about religion.
Socrates had been a priest of Athens.
Plato had asked for a religious trial.
The amnesty barred charges for acts during the tyranny, so a different charge was needed to reach a man linked to Critias and Alcibiades.

questions.feedback_general: Critias and Alcibiades had been companions of Socrates, and many Athenians linked him to them. The amnesty meant no one could be tried for acts during the tyranny, so some historians think a religious charge was a way around that rule.

questions.text: Aristotle taught that human beings are made to live in a polis. Which statement would he be most likely to agree with?

answers.text: A person who could never live in any city would lose the chance to become fully good.
A person is best off living alone and far from other people.
Only rulers need to be good, because everyone else simply obeys.
A city should care only for its richest citizens.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Aristotle held that the polis is the only place where a person can fully become good. He also taught that any form of rule is good when it cares for the whole people and bad when it cares only for the rulers.

quizzes.title: 25.2 Reading Quiz: Sparta's Empire and Thebes's Moment

questions.text: Many Greek cities had been told that Sparta fought to set Greece free. Why did they come to hate Sparta within a few years?

answers.text: Sparta charged them higher taxes than Athens ever had.
Sparta put friendly oligarchs in power and placed garrisons in some cities, so it acted as a new master.
Sparta refused to fight against anyone.
Sparta gave every city a democracy.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Spartan officers gave orders where Athenian ones had given them before. Spartiates had trained for war and not for ruling other people gently.

questions.text: Under the King's Peace, the Persian king told the Greeks where their borders lay. What does this show about the Greeks?

answers.text: Their quarrels let a foreign king decide matters they had once fought to defend.
They had defeated Persia again and demanded land.
They no longer cared about their own cities.
They had agreed to give up their language.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says that at Marathon and Salamis Greeks had fought so that Persia would not rule them. Now the Great King could tell them where their borders lay. They had won the war against Persia but lost the peace to their own quarrels.

questions.text: At Leuctra, Epaminondas packed his best men fifty rows deep and aimed them at the Spartan king. Why did this plan work?

answers.text: It tricked the Spartans into thinking the Thebans were retreating.
It gave the Thebans more men than the Spartans had in total.
It put overwhelming force against the strongest part of the Spartan line, and Spartans were not used to losing.
It kept the Sacred Band out of the fighting.

questions.feedback_general: The Spartans put their best men on their right, twelve rows deep, as was usual. Epaminondas did the opposite and struck exactly where the Spartans were strongest. The lesson calls it a case where a brilliant idea changed history.

questions.text: Why was freeing Messenia such a heavy blow to Sparta?

answers.text: It gave Thebes control of the Spartan fleet.
It forced Sparta to join the Persian king.
It turned the Spartiates into farmers.
Sparta lost much of its land and the helots who grew its food, and its power never came back.

questions.feedback_general: The Spartiates were soldiers and the helots grew their food. Without Messenia, Sparta lost much of its land and its workers. The lesson says its power never came back.

questions.text: Xenophon says there was even more confusion in Greece after Mantinea than before. What does this suggest about Thebes's attempt to lead?

answers.text: Thebes ruled Greece peacefully for centuries.
Other cities would not accept Thebes as leader, just as they had refused Sparta and Athens, so no one could bring order.
The Persians took over the leadership of Greece.
The Greeks agreed that Sparta should lead again.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Thebes thought it should lead Greece, but other cities would not accept it. Epaminondas died at Mantinea, and the lesson ends with the Greeks tired, divided, and without a leader.

quizzes.title: 26.1 Reading Quiz: Philip II and the Macedonian Machine

questions.text: Philip spent some years as a hostage in Thebes, when Epaminondas was making that city great. What can we reasonably infer about the effect on Philip?

answers.text: He grew to hate all Greek cities.
He learned nothing there that he later used.
He decided to give up the throne.
He likely saw how a trained army could beat a larger one, and he later put that idea to use.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Philip saw how a trained army could beat a bigger one, but adds that we cannot be sure what he learned. The inference is a fair one because he went on to rebuild the Macedonian army.

questions.text: Philip's foot soldiers carried the sarissa, a pike more than twelve feet long, and nobles rode beside them as the Companion cavalry. How did the two parts work together?

answers.text: The pike line held the enemy in place, and the cavalry struck at the weak spot or the side.
The cavalry held the enemy in place, and the pikes chased them down.
Both stayed behind the walls of the city.
The pikemen and horsemen took turns fighting every battle.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson calls the pike line a moving wall that enemies could not easily reach. The pikemen did not have to win alone. They only had to hold the enemy while the cavalry rode around and hit from the side.

questions.text: Philip took the city of Amphipolis and the gold mines near it. Why did that matter so much to his plans?

answers.text: The mines gave Macedonia a famous harbor.
Greek cities refused to trade with him without it.
A full-time, paid army was costly, and the gold gave him steady money for coins and wages.
It let him avoid ever using diplomacy.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says such an army cost a lot of money, and that the gold from the mines paid for it. It also says Philip used diplomacy, marriages, and treaties alongside the army.

questions.text: Demosthenes urged Athenian citizens to serve in the army themselves instead of hiring mercenaries. What did he believe?

answers.text: That Athens should make peace with Philip at once.
That freedom must be defended by citizens who are willing to give up comfort, time, and money.
That the Athenian fleet was too small to matter.
That the festivals should be made longer.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Demosthenes was not trying to frighten people for no reason. He thought freedom must be defended by citizens, and he complained that Athenians preferred festivals to war.

questions.text: After Chaeronea, the Greek states kept running their own affairs at home. What had changed for them?

answers.text: They had to give up their gods.
They no longer had any assemblies at all.
They became part of Persia.
They could no longer decide questions of war and peace for themselves.

questions.feedback_general: Philip called the states together at Corinth, and they agreed to keep the peace among themselves and to follow him against Persia. The cities were still there, but they now followed a king.

quizzes.title: 26.2 Reading Quiz: Alexander Invades Persia

questions.text: When Thebes revolted in 335 BC, Alexander destroyed the city. What did the rest of Greece take from this?

answers.text: That Alexander was too busy to answer revolts.
That Athens would soon take Thebes's place.
That revolt against the new king would be punished harshly, and the revolts stopped.
That Sparta would come to their aid.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the rest of Greece took the lesson and the revolts stopped. It adds that the act was ruthless and that Alexander could be kind and cruel in the same year.

questions.text: At Issus the armies met on a narrow plain between the mountains and the sea. Why did that help Alexander?

answers.text: The Persians had no horses.
Darius was not present at the battle.
The Greeks were fighting at home.
In such a tight space, the Persians could not use their much larger numbers.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the Persians could not use their big numbers on a narrow plain. Historians still ask why Darius chose to fight in that place instead of waiting on open ground.

questions.text: After Issus, Alexander did not chase Darius. He went south to take the great port cities. What was his reason?

answers.text: The Persian fleet was crewed by men from those cities, so without the ports it would have nowhere to land.
He wanted to spend the winter near Athens.
He had promised the priests of Egypt that he would visit.
He was afraid of Darius's army.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says that without the ports the Persian fleet had nowhere to go. That is why Tyre mattered, even though it took seven months and a causeway of rubble to win it.

questions.text: Egypt welcomed Alexander. Which of the following helps explain why?

answers.text: Egypt had been a Greek colony for centuries.
The Egyptians had not liked Persian rule, and Egypt's grain and wealth gave Alexander food and money.
The Egyptians feared that Alexander would burn Memphis.
The Persian king had sent his army there to protect it.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says Egypt had disliked Persian rule and was one of the richest lands in the world. Taking it gave Alexander food, money, and safety for his rear.

questions.text: The lesson says Alexander was brave, quick, and trusted by his men, but also lucky. Which statement best fits that view?

answers.text: His victories were certain from the start.
Luck alone explains his victories.
Skill and luck worked together, and a few small changes at the Granicus or Issus might have changed everything.
His army was larger than the Persian army in every battle.

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says that a blow landing a little differently at the Granicus, or a king who waited at Issus, might have changed everything. Historians weigh his skill and the chances of the moment together.
